content: A wiki is a collection of web pages that allows any user with access to contribute to or modify its content. This is achieved through the use of a simplified markup language, which makes editing accessible to a wide range of users. Wikis are commonly employed to create collaborative websites and community-driven platforms. A well-known example of a wiki is Wikipedia, a collaborative encyclopedia. In business settings, wikis are often utilized to establish cost-effective and efficient intranets or to facilitate knowledge management. The first wiki software, WikiWikiWeb, was developed by Ward Cunningham, who described it as the simplest online database that could possibly work. The term wiki originates from the Hawaiian word for fast, and the name WikiWiki was inspired by a shuttle bus at Honolulu International Airport. Cunningham chose this term as an alliterative alternative to quick to avoid naming the system quick-web. His work was partially influenced by Apple’s HyperCard, which allowed users to create virtual card stacks with interlinked content. Cunningham expanded on Vannevar Bush’s ideas by enabling users to comment on and modify each other’s text. In the early 2000s, wikis gained popularity in enterprise environments as collaborative tools for project communication, intranets, and documentation, initially targeting technical users. Today, some companies rely solely on wikis for collaboration, replacing static intranets. Wikis are often more widely used within private networks (behind firewalls) than on the public internet. The term wiki was officially added to the Oxford English Dictionary Online on March 15, 2007. Ward Cunningham and Bo Leuf, in their book The Wiki Way: Quick Collaboration on the Web, outlined the core principles of wikis. Wikis invite all users to edit existing pages or create new ones using a standard web browser without requiring additional software. They promote meaningful associations between topics by making it easy to create links between pages and indicate whether a target page exists. Wikis are not designed as polished sites for casual visitors but rather as dynamic platforms for ongoing creation and collaboration. They enable collaborative document creation using a simple markup language, often referred to as wikitext. A single page within a wiki is called a wiki page, while the entire interconnected collection of pages is referred to as the wiki. Wikis function as databases for creating, browsing, and searching information, with a defining feature being the ease of page creation and updates. Most wikis allow real-time edits that appear almost instantly online, though this openness can lead to potential misuse. Private wikis often require user authentication for editing or even reading content. Editing wiki pages typically involves a simplified markup language, such as starting a line with an asterisk to create a bulleted list. The syntax of wikitext varies across implementations, with some allowing HTML tags. This approach simplifies editing compared to HTML, which can be cryptic and difficult to modify. While limiting access to HTML and CSS restricts user control over formatting, it ensures consistency in appearance and prevents the implementation of potentially disruptive code. Many wikis now offer WYSIWYG (What You See Is What You Get) editing, which translates graphical formatting instructions (e.g., bold or italics) into HTML or wikitext. However, WYSIWYG editors may not support all features available in wikitext. Some wiki platforms, like MediaWiki, allow users to provide an edit summary to explain changes, which is stored alongside the page revision. Most wikis maintain a record of all changes, enabling users to revert to previous versions if necessary. Navigation within wikis is often facilitated by numerous hypertext links between pages, supporting non-linear exploration. Users can create index or table-of-contents pages with hierarchical categorization, though maintaining these manually can be challenging. Many wikis offer features for categorizing or tagging pages to aid in organization. Backlink features allow users to see which pages link to the current page. Wikis often encourage the creation of links to non-existent pages as an invitation for others to contribute content. Links in wikis are created using specific syntax, such as CamelCase, which capitalizes words and removes spaces (e.g., TableOfContents). While CamelCase simplifies linking, it can result in non-standard spelling. Many modern wikis now use free linking with brackets and disable CamelCase by default. Most wikis provide at least a title search, and some offer full-text search capabilities. The efficiency of searches depends on whether the wiki engine uses a database. Indexed database access is essential for high-speed searches in large wikis. External search engines like Google can sometimes be used for more precise results, though their indexes may be outdated. Wiki software is a type of collaborative software that allows web pages to be created and edited using a common web browser. It is typically implemented as a software engine running on one or more web servers, with content stored in a file system and changes tracked in a relational database. Personal wikis, such as WikidPad and VoodooPad, can run as standalone applications on a single computer. Wikis are designed with the philosophy of making it easy to correct mistakes rather than preventing them. Most wikis feature a Recent Changes page that lists recent edits, allowing users to monitor and verify the validity of new contributions. Additional tools, such as revision history and diff features, enable users to compare changes between versions and restore previous versions if necessary. Some wikis provide content monitoring tools to ensure quality and alert users to modifications. Publicly editable wikis face criticism for their susceptibility to tampering, but proponents argue that the community can identify and correct malicious content. Larger wikis often employ bots to detect and revert vandalism and use JavaScript enhancements to highlight changes. The level of vandalism a wiki experiences depends on its openness. For example, some wikis allow anonymous edits, while others restrict editing to registered users. Closed wikis are more secure but grow slowly, while open wikis grow rapidly but are more vulnerable to vandalism. Wiki communities vary widely, with some being private and used for internal documentation within organizations. Public wikis like Wikipedia benefit from their open nature, which drives growth, while specialized wikis focus on niche topics. WikiNodes are pages that describe related wikis, organized as neighbors or delegates. Domain names containing wiki are increasingly popular for niche communities. Publicly available wiki farms allow users to create their own wikis, with some offering private, password-protected options. Examples include PeanutButterWiki, Socialtext, Wetpaint, and Wikia. Free wiki farms often include advertising on their pages. The English-language Wikipedia has the largest user base among wikis and ranks among the top 10 websites globally in terms of traffic. WikiDoc, the original medical wiki, is the largest physician-driven medical textbook, allowing only registered users to contribute.
